newsitem.title: GERMANY: Bonn proposes Buba payout in 2 tranches - newspaper.
newsitem.headline: Bonn proposes Buba payout in 2 tranches - newspaper.

text.p: The Bonn government paper to be discussed by the Bundesbank's central council on Wednesday contains proposals for a revaluation of central bank reserves which will result in a payment to Bonn in two tranches, one in 1997 and one in 1998, a German newspaper reported.
Boersen-Zeitung reported that the paper also included draft wording for a corresponding amendment to Bundesbank legislation.
The newspaper, which did not name its sources, said Bonn had proposed an interim balance sheet which will allow a payment of more than 10 billion marks in 1997.
It also said that neither Finance Minister Theo Waigel nor Juergen Stark, secretary of state at the finance ministry, will attend Wednesday's council meeting.
Boersen-Zeitung also said that there was resistance within the Bundesbank's central council against the plan to have it draw up an interim balance sheet in 1997.
But government sources had said on Tuesday that the Bundesbank was expected to approve the revaluation of its gold reserves.

The gold revaluation plan was part of proposals by Finance Minister Theo Waigel to revalue central bank reserves in a bid to shore up Germany's 1997 budget, straining to meet Maastricht criteria for European monetary union (EMU).

Waigel himself told journalists in Frankfurt on Tuesday that a special interim Bundesbank balance sheet had been drawn up and that as a result Bonn could receive a payout from such reserve revaluations this year.

But his comments came as Bundesbank president Hans Tietmeyer was reported in an unconfirmed newspaper article to have warned Bonn two months ago that any such revaluation in the run-up to EMU risked damaging Germany's credibility.
Government sources said on Tuesday that the central bank would issue a statement after Wednesday's council meeting outlining its position the planned revaluation.

They said the Bundesbank had in principle accepted the plan, announced by Waigel amid great controversy two weeks ago, and that the finance ministry had already informed it of the required changes to the bank's constitution.
The Bundesbank has some 95 million ounces of gold in reserve valued at well below current market levels.
Coalition sources said a revaluation towards market prices could boost federal finances by an extra 10 billion to 12 billion marks in 1997 and by a similar amount in 1998.

Confusion still remains on whether Bonn can in fact use the measure to cut back its 1997 budget deficit to the three percent of gross domestic product (GDP) required for entry into the single European currency.
The Bundesbank's council meeting on Wednesday is one of its regular fortnightly meetings. It has been brought forward by one day because Thursday is a regional holiday in Germany.
